claims.text: Conventional powder processing of W particles in a Cu matrix typically produces interfacial voids and phase separation.
A nanometer-scale metallic coating can be deposited conformally on W particles by atomic layer deposition.
The ALD coating could consist of Cu or a reactive metal that forms a low-melting eutectic with Cu.
Coated W particles can subsequently be processed by Cu infiltration and spark-plasma sintering.
Powder materials can be consolidated by SPS at temperatures below the melting point of major components.
The proposed W–Cu process should use an SPS temperature below the W melting point but above the Cu melting temperature.
A conformal metallic layer on each W particle will enhance metal–metal contact.
The coating will reduce W–Cu interfacial energy and barriers to diffusion.
The coating will produce a continuous, defect-suppressed W–Cu network.
The ALD layer will improve the wetting of W by molten or sintering Cu.
Improved wetting will enhance interfacial diffusion and create a near-perfect W–Cu metallurgical bond.
Improved interfacial bonding will minimize voids and phase-separated regions.
Voids and phase-separated regions are detrimental to thermal transport and mechanical integrity.
Relative to conventionally SPS-processed uncoated W powder, ALD-coated W–Cu will have significantly lower void content.
Relative to the uncoated baseline, ALD-coated W–Cu will have improved microstructural uniformity.
Relative to the uncoated baseline, ALD-coated W–Cu will have greater thermal conductivity.
ALD-coated W–Cu will retain mechanical durability under fusion-relevant irradiation and high-heat-flux conditions.
Excessively thick ALD coatings may alter the balance of thermal and mechanical properties.
